conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and check on how you’re feeling emotionally. I’ll be using a brief, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—to get a clear picture of your mood, anxiety, and overall well-being in these first postpartum weeks.  

Everything you share stays strictly confidential between you and our care team; the goal is simply to make sure you feel heard, supported, and, if needed, connected to the right help quickly. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you today.

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  
<question>Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?</question>

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my partner sent me a silly video of the dog—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. I guess I’d say I haven’t been able to laugh or enjoy things quite as much as before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve been able to laugh a little, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m doing it because I know I should, not because it comes naturally anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Mostly yes—I still plan little outings or coffee with a friend and feel a spark of excitement, but it’s milder than before. Some mornings I just think “what’s the point?” and the enthusiasm fades pretty fast.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, I immediately wonder what I did wrong—like I must be missing some cue or not doing something right. I know it’s probably not fair, but those thoughts still pop up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Every so often I’ll feel my heart race or my mind jumps to “what if something’s wrong with the baby?” even when everything looks fine. It usually passes quickly, but it catches me off guard.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—just a little on-edge here and there. Like, I’ll suddenly worry the baby isn’t breathing when he’s napping, but I can talk myself down pretty fast. It’s more a quick jolt than a real scare.
Things have been getting on top of me

It depends on the day. Sometimes everything feels manageable, but other days—like when the baby won’t nap and the laundry’s piling up—I do feel a bit swamped and think, “How am I supposed to keep doing this?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it hasn’t been that bad. I’ve felt a little down, but I can still fall asleep most nights—maybe just lie there an extra twenty minutes if I’m replaying the day, but I wouldn’t say the unhappiness keeps me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do feel sad or kind of blue a few times a week—nothing crushing, just a heavy “blah” feeling that lingers for a while, especially in the evenings when the house quiets down.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Maybe once or twice this week—usually when I’m overtired and the baby won’t settle. I’ll just tear up for a few minutes, feel a bit better after, but it’s not an all-day thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I’d never want to hurt myself; I just want to feel more like “me” again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, self-report via EPDS-10 follow-up

Symptoms / behavioral concerns endorsed  
- Mild anhedonia: laughter feels forced, anticipatory enjoyment “milder than before”  
- Intermittent low mood: “blah” several evenings/week, situational tearfulness when fatigued  
- Excessive self-blame regarding infant care  
- Episodic, non-persistent anxiety: sudden “what-if” worries about infant safety, quickly self-soothed  
- Variable sense of being overwhelmed, especially when daily tasks accumulate

Patterns  
- Symptoms fluctuate with fatigue/stress; no pervasive day-long despair  
- No current sleep disruption attributable to mood (sleep-onset delay ≤20 min)  
- No anhedonia severe enough to prevent planning or brief pleasant activities  
- No panic attacks or persistent physiological arousal

Screening significance  
- Sub-threshold depressive features (sad mood, crying, anhedonia)  
- Mild perinatal anxiety (situation-specific worries, no avoidance/impairment)  
- Coping resources appear intact (self-soothing, social planning)

Risk factors present  
- Low mood and crying spells, but < daily  
- Self-blame/guilt cognitions  
- Occasional overwhelmed feelings

Risk factors absent  
- No sleep or appetite disturbance linked to mood  
- No feelings of worthlessness or hopelessness  
- No self-harm, suicidal, or infanticidal ideation

Screening observation  
Findings indicate mild, situational depressive and anxiety symptoms commonly observed in the postpartum period; do not meet threshold for major depression or generalized anxiety disorder at this time. Continue monitoring, encourage supportive measures, and re-screen if symptoms worsen, persist >2 wks, or function deteriorates.
